---
title: "Makerspaces and distributed manufacturing in disaster response and preparedness"
author: "Victoria Wenzelmann"
date: "2026-08-21"
description: "Literature Review"
---

Disasters expose a fundamental vulnerability of highly centralized production and supply systems: when transportation routes, manufacturing facilities, or distribution networks are disrupted, access to even relatively simple goods can become constrained [@citekey ]. For communities already experiencing intermittent access to essential services, such disruptions can rapidly compound existing vulnerabilities. In these situations, the ability to produce, repair, adapt, and modify objects locally can become an important component of resilience. Distributed manufacturing approaches address this vulnerability by dispersing production capabilities geographically and enabling locally situated actors to manufacture or repair products closer to where they are needed.
 
Makerspaces provide an existing form of infrastructure through which such distributed capabilities can be organized. Typically equipped with digital fabrication tools such as 3D printers, CNC machines, laser cutters, electronics equipment, and associated tools, makerspaces combine physical production capacity with skills, knowledge, and social networks. Their relevance to disaster response therefore extends beyond the availability of machinery: makerspaces can function as places where technical knowledge is exchanged, solutions are adapted to local conditions, and people with different forms of expertise collaborate on practical problems.
 
The role of maker communities in crisis response became particularly visible during the COVID-19 pandemic. As global supply chains struggled to meet demand for personal protective equipment and other medical supplies, maker communities rapidly developed, adapted, and produced locally manufactured alternatives. Distributed networks shared open designs and manufacturing instructions while individual makerspaces and fabrication facilities produced components according to local needs and available equipment. These activities demonstrated the potential of distributed manufacturing to complement conventional procurement and supply systems when centralized production and distribution are unable to respond quickly enough. At the same time, the pandemic also exposed important limitations, including inconsistent quality, difficulties in validating designs, shortages of raw materials, and challenges in coordinating decentralized production.
 
Similar dynamics can be observed in other disaster and conflict settings. In contexts where infrastructure is damaged or supply routes are interrupted, local repair and fabrication capabilities can provide communities with alternatives to waiting for externally procured goods. Makerspaces and related community workshops have supported the repair of equipment, adaptation of existing technologies, production of spare parts, and development of context-specific solutions. In Ukraine, for example, maker communities and distributed manufacturing initiatives have increasingly contributed to repair, humanitarian production, and the adaptation of technologies to rapidly changing local needs. Such experiences suggest that the value of makerspaces during crises lies not only in their capacity to manufacture objects, but also in their ability to improvise, repair, and recombine available resources in response to problems that cannot always be anticipated in advance.
 
This capacity is closely connected to the concept of distributed manufacturing. Rather than concentrating production in a small number of large facilities, distributed manufacturing enables geographically dispersed production nodes to manufacture similar or locally adapted products using shared digital designs, specifications, and knowledge. Digital fabrication technologies make this model particularly accessible because designs can be transmitted digitally while production takes place locally. In principle, a design developed in one location can therefore be manufactured in another without requiring the physical transportation of the finished product. This creates the possibility of geographically distributed production networks that can continue operating even when individual nodes or parts of the wider supply chain become unavailable.
 
Open hardware strengthens this potential by making designs, documentation, and technical knowledge available for reuse and adaptation. Instead of treating the design as a proprietary component of a centralized production process, open hardware allows distributed actors to access, modify, and manufacture physical artefacts locally. In disaster contexts, this can be particularly valuable because local actors may need to adapt solutions to available materials, tools, environmental conditions, or cultural practices. The combination of open designs and distributed manufacturing thus creates a pathway from globally shared knowledge to locally produced responses.
 
However, the existence of a digital design does not in itself constitute a resilient production system. Distributed manufacturing depends on a range of physical and social conditions: appropriate machinery, materials, electricity, technical skills, maintenance capacity, documentation, quality assurance, and relationships with communities and institutions. These dependencies become especially significant during disasters, precisely when electricity and connectivity may be unreliable, supply chains disrupted, and technical personnel difficult to reach. A manufacturing node that depends on continuous internet access to retrieve designs, centralized cloud services to access documentation, or international supply chains for critical components may therefore remain vulnerable despite being geographically distributed.
 
This points to an important distinction between response capacity and preparedness. Much of the existing literature and many practical initiatives demonstrate that makerspaces can contribute to disaster response once a crisis has occurred. Considerably less attention has been paid to the infrastructure and organizational conditions that allow these capabilities to exist before a crisis. Preparedness requires more than having access to fabrication equipment. It involves maintaining skills, identifying locally relevant needs, preparing and validating designs, ensuring access to materials and tools, establishing relationships between local actors, and making technical knowledge available under conditions in which conventional digital infrastructure may no longer function.
 
The distinction is particularly relevant because disaster response frequently operates under severe time constraints. During an emergency, there may be little opportunity to identify suitable designs, establish manufacturing partnerships, train people to use unfamiliar equipment, or determine whether a locally produced component is fit for purpose. Preparedness therefore shifts some of this work from the moment of response to the period before a disaster occurs. The objective is not necessarily to predict exactly what will be needed, but to establish the capabilities and relationships that allow communities to respond to unforeseen needs.
 
Existing work on makerspaces and distributed manufacturing provides several elements of such a system, but these elements are often treated separately. Research on makerspaces emphasizes community capacity, learning, and grassroots innovation; work on distributed manufacturing focuses on geographically dispersed production and digital fabrication; open hardware research addresses the accessibility and reproducibility of designs; and disaster preparedness research emphasizes risk reduction, planning, and resilience. What remains comparatively underexplored is the intersection of these fields: how open knowledge, local production capacity, resilient connectivity, and community-based infrastructure can be deliberately organized as a distributed preparedness system.
 
This gap is also visible in the temporal dimension of existing approaches. Maker responses to disasters are frequently characterized by rapid mobilization: communities activate existing capabilities when an emergency occurs. A preparedness-oriented approach instead asks what needs to be established, maintained, and shared during periods of relative stability so that these capabilities can be activated when centralized systems fail. In this sense, preparedness is not simply a matter of accumulating physical supplies. It can also be understood as maintaining a distributed capacity to access knowledge, make decisions, produce and repair objects, and coordinate action under disrupted conditions.
 
Makerspaces are particularly relevant to this perspective because they bring together several of these capabilities in a single local setting. They can provide access to tools and machinery, but also to practical knowledge, peer learning, social networks, and locally embedded problem-solving capacity. Their potential role in preparedness therefore extends beyond their function as production facilities. They can serve as nodes within wider networks through which designs, skills, experiences, and production capabilities are shared between locations while remaining locally actionable.
 
At the same time, this potential should not be interpreted as evidence that makerspaces are inherently resilient. Makerspaces themselves can be dependent on fragile infrastructures, external funding, imported equipment and materials, stable electricity, internet connectivity, and a relatively small number of skilled individuals. Treating makerspaces as preparedness infrastructure therefore requires attention to their own vulnerabilities and to the dependencies that connect them to wider systems. The relevant unit of resilience may consequently not be the individual makerspace, but the network of distributed capabilities in which multiple nodes can compensate for, support, or learn from one another.
 
Taken together, the literature points toward a shift in how distributed manufacturing and makerspaces can be understood in disaster contexts. Rather than viewing them solely as emergency production facilities, they can be considered components of a broader infrastructure of preparedness: one that combines locally embedded capabilities with globally shared knowledge and distributed production networks. Such an infrastructure would need to remain useful during normal conditions while also being capable of operating under degraded conditions, including intermittent connectivity, disrupted supply chains, and limited access to external support.
